# Dealing with Text: stringr {#sec-stringr}

<!-- TODO: Teach separate - here or in chapter 7? -->
<!-- TODO: Should we mention str_c(collapse) in summarize()? -->

Many interesting (computational) social science data sets have textual elements.
This can e.g. be the contents of online posts or reviews,
official documents, reports, or party manifestoes,
but also open survey questions or question metadata. 

Very often, we need to clean, preprocess and/or analyse this textual data. 
This chapter will take the first steps in this by introducing the tidyverse `stringr` package,
which can handle most of the cleaning functions such as normalizing, filtering and extracting parts of textual columns. 
In the next chapters we will look at other parts of the pipeline: scraping and reading textual data (@sec-scraping),
analysing Text as Data (@sec-textasdata), and using LLMs as an analysis tool (@sec-llm).

## Chapter objectives {.unnumbered}

In this chapter, you will learn how to use various `stringr` functions for dealing with textual data:

+ Basic text cleaning operations (@sec-basicstringr)
+ Filter data based on the occurrence of specific text (@sec-strdetect)
+ Using basic 'regular expression' patterns to fine, replace or remove parts of a text (@sec-findreplace)
+ Making simple word plots (@sec-wordplots)
+ Optinally, learn regular expression syntax in more detail to make powerful patterns (@sec-regex)

As always, the chapter ends with a [multiple choice quiz](#sec-quizquestions) organized per section that you can use to test your knowledge and understanding. You can also expand the table below to see which functions are covered in this chapter. 


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Functions introduced in this chapter"}

| Function | What it does | Section |
|:-----|:----------|:-----|
| `str_detect()` | does the text contain the pattern? | @sec-strdetect |
| `str_glue()` | build a text, filling in R code between curly braces | @sec-strdetect |
| `str_c(collapse=)` | collapse all values of a vector into a single string | @sec-strdetect |
| `str_to_lower()` | convert text to lower case | @sec-strdetect |
| `str_length()` | the number of characters | @sec-basicfunctions |
| `str_count()` | count how often the pattern occurs in each text | @sec-basicfunctions |
| `str_trim()` | remove whitespace at the start and end | @sec-basicfunctions |
| `str_squish()` | trim and normalize all whitespace in the text | @sec-basicfunctions |
| `str_extract()` | extract the first match in each text | @sec-strextract |
| `str_remove_all()` | remove all matches | @sec-strremove |
| `str_replace_all()` | find and replace | @sec-strreplace |
| `fixed()` | treat the whole pattern as literal text | @sec-strreplace |
| `str_extract_all()` | extract all matches in each text | @sec-extractall |
| `str_view()` | show the matches of a pattern | @sec-specifiers |
| `str_c()` | combine texts into one | @sec-anchors |
| `str_subset()` | only the texts that contain the pattern (for a vector, not a data frame) | @sec-anchors |
| `regex()` | wrap a regular expression to specify options | @sec-anchors |

:::

## Data for this chapter: US Elections on Bluesky {.unnumbered}

As an example data set for this chapter, 
we will use a collection of Bluesky posts about the 2024 US elections (see [the book's github repository](https://github.com/vanatteveldt/r4css/blob/main/data/README.md#us-elections-bluesky-posts) for the R code used to scrape these posts).
To make things easier, we will only keep the date, author and text columns:

```{webr}
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vanatteveldt/r4css/refs/heads/main/data/bluesky_us_elections_2024.csv", "bluesky_us_elections_2024.csv")
posts <- read_csv("bluesky_us_elections_2024.csv")|>
  select(author=author_name, date=created_at, likes=like_count, text)
head(posts)
```

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['demo_detect_trump', 'demo_detect_lower', 'demo_length_likes', 'demo_squish_count', 'demo_pattern_or', 'demo_hashtag_extract', 'demo_hashtag_remove', 'demo_mention_anonymize', 'demo_hashtag_extract_all', 'demo_hashtag_toy', 'demo_dotall', 'wordplot', 'demo_shrug', 'demo_sentiment', 'demo_sentiment2', 'demo_groups']
library(tidyverse)
posts <- read_csv("data/bluesky_us_elections_2024.csv") |>
  select(author=author_name, date=created_at, likes=like_count, text)
sad_words <- c("sad", "weak", "terrible", "disgrace", "disaster", "loser", "stupid", "dishonest", "pathetic", "horrible")
sad_pattern <- str_c("\\b(", str_c(sad_words, collapse="|"), ")\\b")

```

## Using `stringr` for basic text cleaning and processing {#sec-basicstringr}

As a first step, we will look at a number of functions from the `stringr`
package for detecting and counting whether a text contains a specific word or substring. This is very useful for cleaning and exploring data. 

### Who do people post about? Using `str_detect` in `filter` {#sec-strdetect}

A first question we might ask is how much people post about a candidate, for example Donald Trump. We can use `str_detect` to check whether a text contains a specific substring, and use that to filter the posts:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_detect_trump
trump_posts <- posts |> filter(str_detect(text, "Trump"))
head(trump_posts)
str_glue("Total number of posts: {nrow(posts)}")
str_glue("Number of posts about trump: {nrow(trump_posts)}")
```


:::{.callout-note title="str_glue"}
In the example above, we used `str_glue` to display the number of posts in a nice way. You've actually already seen this in @sec-vis-why, where we used it to create a nice label in a graph.

`str_glue` is a very useful function for building a text by 'glueing' calculated values (such as `{nrow(posts)}`) into a text. Technically, all R code within curly braces (`{}`) will be evaluated and inserted into the text. 

A small caveat: if the code produces multiple values, this will result in multiple texts being produced. This is useful if you use `str_glue` within a `mutate` call, as it will produce a value for each row, but might be surprising if you use it to quickly print something like above.
You can use `str_glue("Count to three: {str_c(1:3, collapse=',')}")` if you want to include multiple values in a single string: this 'collapses' multiple values (1, 2 and 3 in this case) into a single string `"1,2,3"`.
:::


As you can see, about 25% of the posts mention Trump -- or rather, contain the specific sequence of characters `T-r-u-m-p`. This will not find `trump`, but will find `#Trump`, `DonaldTrump`. To also find matches of `trump`, an easy trick is to call `str_to_lower(text)` to lowercase the whole text column:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_detect_lower
posts |> filter(str_detect(str_to_lower(text), "trump"))
```

Which finds about 300 extra mentions (which could of course also include false positives, e.g. trump used a verb or trumpet as a musical instrument)

::: {.callout-note title="All the str_ functions"}
As you might have noticed, all functions introduced above started with `str_`:
`str_detect`, `str_glue`, and `str_to_lower`. 
This naming convention holds for (almost) all functions in `stringr`. 
This makes it easy to find them in Rstudio: 
just type `str_` and press tab or control_space, and you get an overview of all 
the functions for dealing with text. 
See the table near the end of this chapter for an overview of useful stringr functions. 
:::

### Basic string functions in a data frame {#sec-basicfunctions}

Next to filtering, it can be useful to use `stringr` within a `mutate` call
to calculate properties of the data. For example, we could count the length of all posts, and check if longer posts get more likes:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_length_likes
posts <- posts |>
  mutate(length=str_length(text))
cor.test(posts$length, posts$likes)
```

We can also use `str_count` to count how often a fragment occurs within a text.
If we count the number of spaces, we get a decent approximation of the number of words in each post (but see the callout below on characters vs words).

Before we do this, we should probably normalize the whitespace in the posts.
The function `str_trim` can be used to remove ('trim') all whitespace at the start and end of a text. 
We will go a step further and use `str_squish`, which trims the text but also replaces all consecutive whitespaces by a single space, i.e. it replaces newlines, tabs, multiple spaces or any combination of these by a single space. 

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_squish_count
posts <- posts |>
  mutate(text_normalized=str_squish(text),
         length=str_length(text_normalized),
         nwords=str_count(text_normalized, " "))
head(posts)
```

### Exercise: Talk of the town?

{{< include exercises/_ch09_ex_mentions_over_time.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis of texts: characters or words?"}

In the examples and exercise above, we use the `str_` functions 
to perform simple text analyses by counting mentions of candidates. 

This works, but has very clear limits because `stringr` fundamentally works on **characters**, while a lot of our analyses talk about words. 
As mentioned, `str_detect(str_to_lower(text), "trump")` will match trumpet
(as well as `"#trump"`, `"STRUMP"` and `"Strumpfhose"`). The reason is that `stringr` sees `Strumpfhose` as a sequence of characters `S-t-r-u-m-p-f...`, and these characters contain the sequence `t-r-u-m-p`, so it matches. `stringr` doesn't really know what a word is, and doesn't really care either. 

This can be solved to a degree by using more sophisticated matching rules, as explained below, but these solutions are relatively brittle and address the sympton rather than the cause: often, we would like to analyse words rather than characters. @sec-textasdata will address this problem head-on by first **tokenizing** a text into words, and then using analyses on the words.

None of this makes the `stringr` package any less relevant:
Functions like `str_detect`, `str_trim` and `str_count` are still very useful for filtering and cleaning texts -- and in fact many of the analyses in @sec-textasdata will use these functions either before or after the tokenization to clean the text and analyse the extracted words. 
:::

## Finding, removing and replacing simple patterns {#sec-findreplace}

The code above showed how you can detect and count literal substrings.
The `stringr` functions are much more powerful than that, however,
as you can also search for *patterns* rather than literal strings.

For now, we will just introduce some very basic patterns, that are however already quite powerful. 
For example, the code below uses the patterns `Trump|Vance`  and `Harris|Walz`, which detect mentions of either of the names:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_pattern_or
rep_posts <- posts |> filter(str_detect(text, "Trump|Vance"))
dem_posts <- posts |> filter(str_detect(text, "Harris|Walz"))
str_glue("Out of {nrow(posts)} posts, {nrow(rep_posts)} mention Trump or Vance, while {nrow(dem_posts)} mention Harris or Walz")
```

So, it looks like the republican ticket gets more attention on Bluesky than the democratic ticket - 
does that necessarily mean that coverage is more favourable for the Trump ticket?

### Extracting a pattern with `str_extract` {#sec-strextract}

Another pattern is `#\\w+`, which matches any word starting with a `#`.  
Using the function `str_extract`, we can use it to extract the (first) hashtag in each post, and store it as a new column:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_hashtag_extract
posts |>
  mutate(tag=str_extract(text, "#\\w+")) |>
  count(tag) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

As you can see, the corpus is dominated by the hashtag `#Election2024`.
This is actually very unsurprising, since that tag was used to select the posts, so each post will contain this tag. 

Note that the reason why the total is lower than the total number of posts is that the code above only extracts the *first* occurrence of a pattern, so in the other posts another tag was used before that tag (and see @sec-extractall for `str_extract_all` to extract all tags)

::: {.callout-note title="Regular expressions?"}
The pattern introduced above (`#\\w+`) may look weird, overly complex, or suspiciously like a cartoon curseword. But it's actually a very standardized and useful way to express character patterns called **regular expressions** (or *regex*, for friends)

Although this will be explained in much more detail in @sec-regex,
it is useful to explain at least a little bit of what is going on. 
In a regex, most characters simply match that character, which is why we could use `"trump"` earlier to simply search for the word "trump", or actually the sequence of characters `t-r-u-m-p`. 

We also saw the special character `|`, which was used to list multiple alternatives. So, `angry|mad|annoyed` would match any of these strings,
but be aware that they match characters, and not words: This pattern would also match `armada`, since it contains the characters `m-a-d`. See @sec-anchors below for a solution.

The `\\w` used in the last example, functions as a kind of wildcard called a *character class*.
Rather than matching a literal sequence of `\` and `w` characters, it matches '**w**ord characters' defined as letters and numbers (and curiously the underscore `_`). So, `#\\w` would match a literal hash sign (`#`), followed by a letter, number, or underscore. Similarly, `\\d` matches **d**igits and `\\s` matches white**s**pace.

The last part, `+`, is a quantifier which reads "one or more": it means that the preceding character (in this case, the `\\w` word character class) is required but may be repeated as often as desired. So, the total pattern `#\\w+` matches a literal hash sign, followed by one or more word characters, which is a fair approximation of a hash tag.

By using combinations of character classes and quantifiers, you can make patterns for many useful things such as hashtags, zip codes, phone numbers, email addresses, etc. See @sec-regex below for more detail.
:::

### Removing parts of a text with `str_remove_all` {#sec-strremove}

Since the occurrence of this particular hashtag is not informative, let's clean the data first by lowercasing it, and then removing that hashtag using `str_remove_all`, followed by the same code as above:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_hashtag_remove
posts |>
  mutate(text=str_to_lower(text),
         text=str_remove_all(text, "#election2024"),
         tag=str_extract(text, "#\\w+")) |>
  count(tag) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

This is more informative: a number of posts had no other hashtags (giving a `NA` for the extraction), and after the somewhat generic `#politics` and `#vote` tags we see hashtags for the two main candidates, mostly balanced. 

### Replacing text with `str_replace_all` {#sec-strreplace}

Next to removing text, we can replace parts of a text with `str_replace_all(text, pattern, replacement)`. For example, we can 'anonymize' the at-mentions by replacing all word characters after an at sign by an `ANONYMIZED` placeholder 
(using `str_squish` to make it easier to read the results):

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_mention_anonymize
posts |>
  filter(str_detect(text, "@\\w+")) |>
  mutate(
    text = str_squish(text),
    anonymized=str_replace_all(text, "@\\w+", "@ANONYMIZED")) |>
  select(anonymized)
```

Note that this only replaces the at-mention until a non-word character appears. Since bluesky names often contain domain names (e.g. `@example.bsky.social`) this will only replace the first part and leave the domain intact,
which might or might not be a desired effect.
For more powerful ways of specifying patterns, see @sec-regex below. 

:::{.callout-note title="Matching periods: escaping and fixed()"}
As noted above, the `\\w` pattern matches letters, numbers, and underscore, but not the dots in a domain name. 
Confusingly, the period character (`.`) also does not (just) match a literal dot:
it is a character class itself, and matches every possible character (apart from line breaks). So,
`@\\w+.bsky.social` matches all at-mentions in this domain, but would also match `@\\w+_bsky_social` and even `@\\w+ bsky social`.

For this case it's probably not a big deal, as those patterns are unlikely to appear. But let's try searching for `U.S.`:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_dotall
us_posts <- posts |> filter(str_detect(text, 'U.S.'))
str_glue("Total number of matches: {nrow(us_posts)}")
print("Text of the 23rd match:")
us_posts$text[23]
```

As you can see, this gives 130 matches. But not all of them actually contain the string `U.S.`, for example the 23rd match printed here. Why did that post match?

The answer, of course, is that `.` is a wildcard, so the pattern `U.S.` matched the word `RUSSIAN`!

To remedy this, you have two options. The easiest is to enclose the whole pattern in a `fixed()` function: `str_detect(text, fixed('U.S.'))` tells R to actually not use a regular expression pattern, but a fixed substring. 
Note that within a `fixed()` everyhing matches literal characters, including `|` and `+`. 
To match literal periods within a more complex pattern, you will have to to place a double backslash before each period: `U\\.S\\.|U\\.\\K\\.`, a practice known as *escaping* (again, see @sec-regex below for more detail). Try either `fixed('U.S.')` or `U\\.S\\.` in the code above - it should return 102 rows instead of the original 130. 

Note that the same logic holds for other 'special' characters, such as brackets (both `()` and `[]`) and the quantifiers `+` and `*`,
so you also need to either wrap the whole pattern in `fixed()` or escape each of those characters if you want to match literal brackets or plus-signs.
:::

### Finding multiple occurrences with `str_extract_all` {#sec-extractall}

Earlier, we tried to analyse hashtag usage in the US Election posts,
noting the limitation that `str_extract` only extracts the first occurrence of a pattern.

After seeing the examples with `str_remove_all` and `str_replace_all`, 
you may have guessed that there is also a function called `str_extract_all` -- and you would be right. 

The complication is that this of course can return multiple results per row, which does not really fit with the idea of a column in a data frame: a cell normally contains only a single value. This can be solved by using `unnest_longer`, for example to do a complete count of all hashtags:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_hashtag_extract_all
hashtags <- posts |>
  mutate(tag=str_extract_all(str_to_lower(text), "#\\w+")) |>
  unnest_longer(tag) |>
  count(tag) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
head(hashtags)
```

Technically, `str_extract_all` produces a 'list column', i.e. a column with a data type list. Since that is not very useful for analysis, we *unnest* the list column into a long format: every value becomes a row, so if two hashtags were found the row will be repeated for each hashtag, with only the `tag` column being different and containing a single tag. 

To make this more explicit, the following toy example shows the results for each step:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_hashtag_toy
toy <- tibble(text="Three hashtags: #trump #harris #biden")
toy <- toy |> mutate(tag=str_extract_all(text, "#\\w+"))
print("Result after extract_all:")
print(toy)

toy <- toy |> unnest_longer(tag)
print("Result after unnest_longer:")
print(toy)
```

## Word plots with `ggrepel` {#sec-wordplots}

Word clouds are a staple of (bad) text analysis blogs,
but that doesn't mean we should never make them. 

### A simple word cloud

In `ggplot`, a word cloud is simply a normal plot, with an aesthetic mapping for the dimensions of the data we want to use. 
The main difference is that we use the `geom_text_repel` from the `ggrepel` package which 'repels' words to try to avoid them overlapping each other. 
For example, using the `hashtags` data frame created earlier, the following code plots a traditional word cloud:

```{webr}
#| exercise: wordcloud
#| setup: true

library(tidyverse)
posts <- read_csv("data/bluesky_us_elections_2024.csv") |>
  select(author=author_name, date=created_at, likes=like_count, text)
hashtags <- posts |>
  mutate(tag=str_extract_all(str_to_lower(text), "#\\w+")) |>
  unnest_longer(tag) |>
  count(tag) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: wordcloud
library(ggrepel)
set.seed(1)
hashtags |>
  filter(tag != "#election2024") |>
  slice_max(order_by=n, n=75, with_ties = FALSE) |> 
  mutate(x=rnorm(n()) / sqrt(n), y=rnorm(n()) / sqrt(n))  |>
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y, size=n, label=tag)) +
    geom_text_repel(min.segment.length=Inf) +
  theme_void() + theme(legend.position="none")
```


Technicalities aside, how informative is the plot we made above?
Could we have made a bar plot with the same information?
Would that make it easier to see what's going on, or harder?

::: {.callout-note title="Why are word clouds so complicated?"}

You might have noticed we are doing quite a lot of work to produce a word cloud:

- `set.seed(1)` is used to fix the random seed so the plot comes out (mostly) deterministically.
- we filter out `#election2024` as this tag was used to collect the data, so every post in the data set will contain that tag.
- we manually calculate a semi-random x and y coordinate for each word, where we use `rnorm(n())` to create a normal distribution around 0, and then divide by `sqrt(n)` to nudge more frequent words closer to the center of the plot.
- The `ggplot` is fairly standard apart from the `geom_text_repel`. This geom essentially places each word on its x and y position, checks if it overlaps a previous word, and then starts moving it away from that word until it doesn't overlap anymore (or it gives up).  
- We set `min.segment.length=Inf` to suppress the use of segments. By default, `ggrepel` will draw a line from the label to the actual x and y position where it started. We don't  want to see those lines so we set the minimum length to infinity.

The main reason for this is that the tool we introduced, `ggrepel`, 
is meant more for flexible plotting of texts than for pure word clouds. 
As we will see below, we can use it to encode more meaning in word plots,
but it is also very useful for annotating e.g. scatter plots by labeling specific points, without creating overlap on the labels. In fact, this is why the 
default draws a line from the 'repelled' label to its intended position. 

If all you want is a word cloud, `ggwordcloud` can probably do this more easily
(and perhaps more beautifully). 
But we hope that after reading this section you won't actually (just) want a word cloud!
:::

### A more informative word plot

The main criticism of word clouds is that they only use a single dimension of the data (frequency), and the rest of the variation (e.g. on the x and y axes) is just random noise. 
However, we can also use other dimensions of the data, such as the date a word is used or the topic or cluster it was used in.  For example, the code below creates an over-time usage word plot of the hashtags dataset created above:

```{webr}
#| exercise: wordplot
set.seed(1)
posts |>
  mutate(tag=str_extract_all(str_to_lower(text), "#\\w+")) |>
  unnest_longer(tag) |>
  filter(tag != "#election2024") |>
  group_by(tag) |>
  # (1) compute median date and number of authors per tag
  summarize(n=n_distinct(author), date=median(date)) |>
  # (2) Select top-5 tags per week
  mutate(week=floor_date(date, "week")) |>
  slice_max(order_by=n, n=5, by=week, with_ties=FALSE) |>
  mutate(y = rnorm(n()) / sqrt(n)) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=date, y=y, size=n, label=tag, color=tag)) +
  # (3) allow for more iterations and time
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(max.overlaps=Inf, min.segment.length=Inf, 
                           max.iter = 100000, max.time=2, direction="y") + 
  scale_x_datetime(expand=expansion(mult=0.1), name="") +
  labs(title="Hashtags used in the 2024 US elections",
       subtitle="Tags displayed on or near their median date of use",
       caption="Source: Bluesky posts via API") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")
```

What can you see in this plot? Do you see different tags before and after the election? Is this plot more informative than a 'regular' word cloud?

This code looks very complicated, but most of it builds on the code used earlier. Have a good look at the individual steps, which should all look familiar. 

That said, we used some particular tricks to make this graph informative:

1. We calculate the median date for each word. This has a tendency to place words near the middle, so the modal date or the date in which it was most dominant would be good alternatives. We also count distinct authors per tag to avoid having a single author dominate the findings.  
2. Since most posts occur around election day, plotting the same top-75 most frequent tags will cause most tags to crowd around that day, and leave especially the post-election coverage almost empty. For that reason, we take the top-5 tags per week rather than the top-75 tags in total, assuring an even distribution over the graph.
3. We tweak the geom to give it more time to converge. Since it functions by moving each individual word until it reaches a place without overlap, it can take quite a number of iterations ('nudges') before each word found a suitable location (and even with these settings, it's quite possible there will still be some overlap). We also set `direction='y'` - this causes the words to be nudged only on the vertical axis, guaranteeing that they are displayed on the correct date. 


## A deep dive into regular expressions {#sec-regex}


In the sections above we have seen a number of `stringr` functions to deal with textual data in R. 
For example, we've used `str_detect` to filter data on whether a term occurs in it, `str_replace_all` and `str_remove_all` to replace or remove specific words or patterns, and `str_extract` to extract patterns such as hashtags. 
As explained above, these functions all use *regular expression patterns* as their driver,
but although we used some patterns (such as `#\\w+` for hashtags), we did not really spend a lot of time on how regular expressions work.

This section will remedy this, and by the end of this section you should have a very good idea of how regular expressions work.
You will also get a fairly complete overview of all the various character classes and other options.

This section uses `str_view` as an important visualization and debugging tool: it simply shows all matches of a pattern in a specified input, making it easy to check and debug regular expressions. 
There are also many useful online tools for analysing regular expressions, such as [regex101.com](https://regex101.com/r/iFqxCV/1), which explains the components of a pattern and lets you test your own patterns, and visualizers such as [regex-vis.com](https://regex-vis.com/?r=%23%28kam%5Bae%5Dla%7Cwalt%3Fz%29%5Cd*%5Cb), which show a visualization of a pattern. Note that for such tools you should use single backslashes rather than double backslashes, so `#\w` instead of `#\\w`.

Note that this section will be a bit more of a reference work and explainer than an interactive tutorial.
So, you might wish to skip the section now, and simply return to it when you need to use more complicated patterns. 
But if you were getting curious about questions like "how do we match words instead of characters",
"what other things are there except for \\w and \\d", or "can we make a perfect pattern for matching emails", read on!


::: {.callout-note title="So how do regular expressions actually work?"}

Each element of a regular expression pattern can have one of three functions:

- It can *specify* what to match, e.g.  a literal character (e.g. `w` matches "w") or a character class (e.g. `\\w` matches any word character). 
- It can *anchor* a match at a specific position: `^cat` matches "cat" only at the start of the text, and `\\bcat` matches "cat" only as the start of a word.  
- It can *quantify* the preceding character: `+` means one or more of the preceding match, so `w+` is one or more "w"s, while `\\w+` means one or more word characters.
- It can *combine* parts of a pattern using parentheses `()` and `|`-alternatives

These can be combined in various ways. For example, you can read `#(trump|vance)\\d+` as "A literal hash sign, followed by either trump or vance, followed by one or more digits", so it would match e.g. `#trump2024` or `#vance24`.

The remainder of this section will discuss each of those functions in turn, and end with a reference list of `stringr` functions and regular expression syntax. 
:::

### Specifiers: Matching literals and character classes {#sec-specifiers}

In the earlier sections of this chapter, we've seen that alphanumerical characters match that literal character, so `c` matches "c" and `cat` matches "cat". 

We've also introduced *character classes* such as `.`, which matches everything (except newline), and `\\w` which matches word characters. There are a couple more classes like `\\w`, such as `\\d` for digits and `\\s` for whitespace. They can also be negated by capitalizing them: `\\W` matches everything *except* for word characters. 

A flexible way to make character classes is to use square brackets: `[abc]` matches a, b, or c, and `[A-Z]` matches all capital letters (but not accented letters like Ç or É). You can also negate these patterns: `[^A-Z]` matches everything except capital letters.  

Every specifier can be quantified, so `\\w+` means one or more word characters, and `[A-Z]{2}` means two  upper case Latin letters. We can use this for example to recognize things like at-mentions, email address, and zip codes:

```{webr}
#| exercise: ['str_view', 'demo_greedy']
#| setup: true
library(stringr)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: str_view
texts <- c("An X at-mention:   @vanatteveldt",
           "A Bsky at-mention: @vanatteveldt.com",
           "An email address:  wouter.van.atteveldt@vu.nl",
           "American zip code: 90210",
           "Extended zip code: 90210-4400",
           "Dutch postal code: 1015 GK")
str_view(texts, "@\\w+", html=TRUE, match=NA)
```

Note: this uses the `str_view` function to show all matches in the specified input texts.
The option `html=TRUE` creates html output that works well in this interactive website,
and `match=NA` indicates that we want to see all input texts, even if they didn't match the pattern.

::: {.challenge}
Can you edit the chunk above to make patterns for: 

- American zip codes (5 digits)
- Extended American zip codes (5 digits, a dash, 4 digits)
- Dutch postal codes: 4 digits, a space, two upper case Latin letters
- Bluesky mentions with domain: An at-sign, one or more word characters, a literal period, one or more word characters
- Generic mentions: An at sign, and one or more word characters or literal periods. Hint: you can use abbreviations like `\\w` within a `[]`-character class. Make sure to escape the period, even within a `[]`-class.
- Simplified email: One or more word characters or periods, an at sign, one or more word characters or period, a literal period, and two or more word characters (hint: two or more can be specified as one followed by one or more)

What would be needed to find at-mentions without also matching the second half of the email address? 

:::

Another powerful way to specify characters is using `\\p{}` for [Unicode categories](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr44/#General_Category_Values). For example, use `\\p{letter}` for letters (including accented or non-Latin letters), `\\p{uppercase_letter}` for upper case letters or `\\p{punctuation}` for punctuation. Besides the general categories listed in the link above, there are also properties for specific scripts. For example, `\\p{hangul}` matches letters in Korean script. Other properties include `\\p{extended_pictographic}` which matches emoji (confusingly `\\p{emoji}` also matches digits as these can be used in constructing emoji like 1️⃣). Unicode properties can be negated by capitalizing: `\\P{letter}` matches everything except for letter characters

We saw earlier that you need to escape special characters such as periods: `.` matches all characters, but `\\.` matches a literal period, and the same for `\\*`, `\\[` etc. Confusingly, to produce a literal backslash you need to use `\\\\`: you escape the backslash itself, and then double up all the backslashes. The reason you need to double the backslashes is that R also parses the string before passing it on to the regular expression engine, so R parses `\\\\` as two backslashes, which is then interpreted by the regex engine as a literal backslash. To ease this burden for complex patterns you can also use raw strings: `r"(U\.S\.)"` is read by R without interpreting the escapes, so it results in the string `U\.S\.`. 

As an example of how hard it can become to read heavily escaped text, let's search for 
shrug emoticons in the Bluesky posts:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_shrug
posts |> filter(str_detect(text, "¯\\\\_\\(ツ\\)_/¯"))
```

Can you rewrite this to use `fixed()` or `r"(...)"`?


### Anchors: Word and text boundaries  {#sec-anchors}

Earlier we showed that you could use `|` to make a simple dictionary of terms to match.
However, something like `angry|mad|annoyed` is problematic as it matches characters, not words.
So, `mad` also matches "ar**mad**a". You could of course start the pattern with a whitespace character,
but that would fail if it is at the start of the text or following punctuation. 

To solve this, we can use `\\b` to match a word **b**oundary, defined as the boundary
between a word character and a non-word character (or the start or end of a text),
which for languages that separate words with spaces works fairly well. 

So, `\\b(angry|mad|annoyed)\\b` would match these three words only if they are separate words,
and if you omit the closing `\\b` it will match any words starting with these terms. 
Let's build a dictionary containing a set of Trump's favorite words:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_sentiment
sad_words <- c("sad", "weak", "terrible", "disgrace", "disaster", "loser", "stupid", "dishonest", "pathetic", "horrible")
sad_pattern <- str_c("\\b(", str_c(sad_words, collapse="|"), ")\\b")
print(sad_pattern)
```

Now, we can use that dictionary with `str_extract` or `str_count` as above to do a sentiment analysis.
But let's first check the top 10 matches of this dictionary to do a face validity check:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_sentiment2
str_subset(str_to_lower(posts$text), sad_pattern) |>
  head(10) |>
  str_view(sad_pattern, html=TRUE)
```

In this example, we first use `str_subset` to select those `posts$text` that contain the pattern,
then take the top-10 with `head` and display the matches with `str_view` as above. 

:::{.challenge}
Did it look like the dictionary was correctly capturing posts mentioning negative emotions?
Can you improve it?

If you replace `head(10)` by `sample(10)`, you get a new sample of matched posts every time you run it. 
Does that help in estimating the validity of the dictionary?

Can you count the percentage of posts that contain a 'sad word'? 
Hint: use `mutate` and `str_detect` or  `str_count` to determine matches, 
and then `summarize` to compute the mean. 
:::

Next to the word boundary anchor, there are two special anchors that match only the start of a text
(`^`) or the end of a text (`$`). So, if you want to know which posts start with 'RT', you can use `^RT` to match those two characters at the start of a post only (an older Twitter convention to mark a retweet).

Note that it may seem that anchors are very similar to character classes.
However, what sets them apart is that anchors don't actually match (or *consume*) a character.
Instead, they point to a point between two characters.
For that reason, you also cannot quantify anchors,
and within `[]` their meaning shifts: as we saw earlier, the `^` in `[^A-Z]` actually negates the character class, and the `$` in `[0-9$]` is just a literal dollar sign. 

:::{.callout-note title="regex flags"}

We noted earlier that `.` matches everything *except newlines*. 
In fact, whether it should match newlines or not is controlled by an option you can set.
To set it, you need to wrap your pattern in a `regex()` function.
So, while normally `<script>.*</script>` would only match a script that is fully contained on a single line,
`regex("<script>.*</script>", dotall=TRUE)` sets the `dotall` flag, 
which causes `.` to also match newlines.
Two other useful flags are `multiline`, which if set makes `^` and `$` also match the start and end of lines; and `ignore_case`, which makes the regular expression ignore case.

These options seem very useful, but in most cases preprocessing your data with `str_squish`
and/or `str_to_lower` achieves the same aims while re-using a general part of your text cleaning pipeline.
So practically, the `regex` flags are not actually used that much. 
:::

### Quantifiers: How many cats do we need? {#sec-quantifiers}

We earlier used `#\\w+` to match hashtags, reading the `+` as "one or more (word characters)". 
`+` is an example of a quantifier, which indicates how many of the preceding part of the pattern should be matched. Next to `+`, you can also use `*`, meaning "zero or more": `#trump\\d*` would match `#trump24`, `#trump2020` but also plain `#trump` as the digits are optional. 

In addition, `?` means "zero or one", making the preceding element optional. So, if we are afraid that people might misspell Tim Walz' last name, we could use `walt?z`, meaning `w-a-l`, followed optionally by a `t`, followed by a `z`.  

Finally, you can specify exactly how many matches you expect using curly braces: `\\d{2}` means exactly two digits, `\\d{2,4}` means two to four digits, and `\\d{2,}` means two of more digits. 
Note that you can also apply quantifiers to character classes, so e.g. `[A-Z]{2}` means exactly two upper case (Latin) letters.


#### Exercise: British postal codes

{{< include exercises/_ch09_ex_postcodes.qmd >}}

Suppose we would look for a .com website domain using a pattern like `https://.*\\.com`. 
This may look reasonable, but in practice this can lead to unexpected results:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_greedy
text <- "See https://r4css.vanatteveldt.com or https://example.com"
str_view(text, "https://.*\\.com", html=TRUE)
```

As you can see, this matches from the first `https://` to the second `.com`,
rather than matching each URL separately. 
The reason for this is that quantifiers are by default *greedy*. This means that, given the choice,
they try to match as much as possible. Since it can validly match `.*` all the way to (just before)
the second `.com`, this is what it will do. 

The remedy is to add a question mark next to the quantifier: `.*?` is a non-greedy version of `.*`.
Try changing it in the code above!

Note that `https://.*?\\.com` is still a pretty bad pattern (try changing `vanatteveldt.com` to `vanatteveldt.nl` above to see what happens). A better pattern would probably be adding a word boundary anchor next to it and/or restricting the character class to e.g. only words and periods: (`https://[\\w.]+\\.com\\b`). Note that the `.` within a `[]`-class does not need to be escaped, and that the `?` is no longer needed as the restricted character class already prevents a 'runaway' greedy match. 


### Groups and alternatives {#sec-groups}

Earlier, we've seen that `#(trump|harris)\\b` would match either `#trump` or `#harris`. 
This is a combination of two mechanisms: `|` is used to indicate two or more alternative patterns that can be matched, and `()` *groups* these alternatives so the parts outside the brackets (`#` and `\\b`)
are not included in the scope of the `|`. 

Another use of groups is that they can be quantified. So, `#(lol)+\\b` would match "#lol" as well as "#lollollol" (but not "#lolll"), and `#trump(2024)?\\b` would match either "#trump" or "#trump2024".

Finally, groups can be used in `str_extract` to specify what should be extracted. 
For example, let's construct a (somewhat complicated) pattern to extract the domains that are linked to in the Bluesky posts:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_groups
start <- "\\b(www\\.|https?://)"
subdomains <- "([\\w.-]+\\.)?"
domain <- "([\\w-]+\\.\\w{2,})"
pattern <- str_c(start, subdomains, domain)

print(str_glue("Domains found by `{pattern}`:"))
posts |> mutate(domain = str_extract(text, pattern, group=3)) |>
  count(domain) |> 
  arrange(desc(n))
```

This pattern looks complicated, but as always if you read it step by step from the left, it starts making sense:

- First, the start of the match needs to be a 'word' starting with either "www.", "https://", "http://" (with `?` making the "s" optional). 
- Next, we allow one or more subdomains to be specified with `[\\w.-]+`, i.e. one or more word characters, dots, or hyphens, and the whole subdomain string has to be followed by a dot. This whole part is made optional: the `?` quantifier applies to the whole parenthesized group.
- The next part is the actual domain, which we define here as one or more word characters or hyphens, followed by a dot, followed by two or more word characters.

This is then merged into a single pattern with `str_c`. Note that this is equivalent
to writing the whole expression as a single pattern directly, but by splitting it up it remains at least somewhat readable. 

As you can see, the actual result of `str_extract` in this case is not the whole hyperlink, but only the domain part. The reason for this is that we wrapped the domain part in parentheses, turning it into a group; and then we specified `group=3` in `str_extract`, which points to this group. It is the third group because both start and subdomains also use groups (to scope the `|` and `?`), so these are groups 1 and 2. 

Two final things to note:

- You can also use so-called *non-capturing groups* by using `(?: )` instead of `()`. For example, try changing start to  `\\b(?:www\\.|https?://)` in the code above, and do the same for subdomains, and then change the group into `group=1` -- it should give the same result. The benefit is that the number of the group we care about (domain) no longer shifts around depending on the rest of the pattern, but perhaps at the cost of further complicating the pattern. 
- Capturing groups can also be used in `str_replace` and `str_detect` by using `\\1` to refer back to group 1. For example, `str_replace_all(text, pattern, "[\\3]")` would use the pattern above to replace all hyperlinks to their domain contained in square brackets, so "Watch https://www.youtube.com now!" becomes "Watch [youtube.com] now!", which could be useful for e.g. anonymizing or normalizing posts or open ended survey responses.

:::{.callout-note title="What is 'regular' about these expressions?"}

As a complete aside: Why are 'regular expressions' called 'regular'? 

The answer goes all the way back to the early days of computers and computer science in the 1950s. A mathematician named Stephen Kleene proposed 'regular languages' and proved that they can be identified by what is called a 'finite state machine': a simple program that has a finite number of states, and can go from one state to another by consuming an input.

What this means for regular expressions is that we can visualize a regex as a finite state machine, 
which provides a nice visual idea of what a pattern does. 
For example, the pattern `#(kam[ae]la|walt?z)\\d*` can be visualised as follows:

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
  S(( )) -->|"#35;"| H(( ))
  H -->|k| K1(( ))
  K1 -->|a| K2(( ))
  K2 -->|m| K3(( ))
  K3 -->|a| K4(( ))
  K3 -->|e| K4(( ))
  K4 -->|l| K5(( ))
  K5 -->|a| F((( )))
  H -->|w| W1(( ))
  W1 -->|a| W2(( ))
  W2 -->|l| W3(( ))
  W3 -->|t| W4(( ))
  W4 -->|z| F
  W3 -->|z| F
  F -->|"\d"| F
```

So, you start from the left by matching a '#'. Then, the pattern diverges: you match either a 'k' or a 'w', and then you have to continue in that branch. Options or alternatives (`[ae]` or `t?`) are depicted as small subbranches, and the final zero or more digits (`\\d*`) is visualized by optionally going into an infinite loop of `\\d`s, with the double circle indicating valid end nodes. 

Because regular expressions can be matched in a single forward pass through the text, 
regular expression matching is generally quite efficient 
(with the small note that later additions such as the `\\1` backreferences briefly mentioned in  @sec-groups actually mean that modern regular expression engines work a bit differently, 
so some patterns can actually cause matches to be somewhat slow)

:::

## Regular expression reference and example patterns

Below are tables with an overview of the most commonly used functions and regular expression syntax.
See also the [stringr cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/strings.pdf).

### Example patterns

Below are some examples of regular expressions for common patterns like dates or HTML tags.

::: {.reftable}

| Goal | Pattern | Example |
|:-----|:--------|:--------|
| US zip code | `\\d{5}` | "90210" |
| US phone number | `(\\d{3}-)?\\d{3}-\\d{4}` | "202-456-1111", "456-1111" |
| Dutch postal code | `\\d{4} ?[A-Za-z]{2}` | "1015 GK" |
| ISO date | `\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}` | "2020-07-20" |
| German date | `\\d{1,2}\\.\\d{1,2}\\.\\d{4}` | "25.6.1988" |
| Year (1900--2099) | `\\b(19|20)\\d{2}\\b` | "2024" |
| Percentage | `\\d+(\\.\\d+)?%` | "48.3%" |
| Amount in dollars | `\\$\\d+(,\\d{3})*(\\.\\d{2})?` | `"$1,250.00"` |
| International phone number | `\\+(\\d[- ]?){7,}\\d` | "+1 555-1234567" |
| URL | `https?://\\S+` | "https://example.com?a=b" |
| E-mail address | `[\\w.-]+@[\\w.-]+\\.\\w+` | "jane.doe@example.com" |
| Hashtag | `#\\w+` | "#election2024" |
| At-mention (including Bluesky domains) | `@[\\w.-]+` | "@vanatteveldt.com" |
| Emoji | `\\p{Extended_Pictographic}` | "😀" |
| HTML tags | `</?\\w[^>]*>` | `"</html>"` |
| HTML character escapes | `&[^;]+;` | `"&nbsp;"` |

: Example patterns {#tbl-regexamples}

:::

::: {.reftable}

| Pattern | Matches | Example |
|:----------|:--------|:--------|
| `a` | the literal character a | `cat` matches "cat" |
| `\\.` | a literal special character (also `\\*`, `\\(`, `\\\\`, ...) | `U\\.S\\.` matches "U.S." |
| `.` | any character except a newline | `c.t` matches "cat", "cot", "c t" |
| `\\w` | a word character: letter, digit or underscore | `#\\w` matches "#e" in "#election" |
| `\\d` | a digit | `\\d\\d` matches "12" or "99" |
| `\\s` | whitespace: space, tab, newline | `a\\sb` matches "a b" |
| `\\W`, `\\D`, `\\S` | anything *except* a word character, digit or whitespace | `\\W` matches the period in "U.S" |
| `[...]` | any one of the listed characters or ranges | `[aeiou]` matches a vowel, `[A-Z0-9]` a capital or digit |
| `[^...]` | any character *except* the listed ones | `[^aeiou]` matches anything but a vowel |
| `\\p{...}` | a character from a [Unicode category](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr44/#General_Category_Values) | `\\p{letter}` matches "a", but also "É" and "조" |
| `\\P{...}` | any character *not* in a Unicode category | `\\P{letter}` matches "1" and "!" |
| `\\b` | word boundary anchor | `\\bcat\\b` matches "cat" as a word, but not in "cats" or "muscat"  |
| `^` | start of text anchor | `^RT` matches RT at the start of a text |
| `$` | end of text anchor | `!$` matches an exclamation mark at the end of a text |


: What to match: character classes and anchors {#tbl-specifiers}
:::


::: {.reftable}

| Pattern | Matches | Example |
|:----------|:--------|:--------|
| `*` | zero or more of the preceding part | `#trump\\d*` matches "#trump" and "#trump2024" |
| `+` | one or more of the preceding part | `#\\w+` matches "#election2024" |
| `?` | zero or one of the preceding part (i.e. optional) | `walt?z` matches "walz" and "waltz" |
| `{n}` | exactly *n* of the preceding part | `\\d{4}` matches "2024" |
| `{n,m}` | between *n* and *m* of the preceding part | `[A-Z]{1,2}` matches "M" and "EH" |
| `{n,}` | *n* or more of the preceding part | `\\w{2,}` matches words of at least two characters |
| `*?`, `+?`, `??` | a lazy quantifier: match as *little* as possible | `https://.*?\\.com` stops at the first ".com" |
| `a|b` | either the pattern on the left or the one on the right | `trump|vance` matches "trump" and "vance" |
| `(...)` | a group, to scope `|`, apply a quantifier, or extract a part | `#(trump|harris)\\b`, `#(lol)+`, `str_extract(text, pattern, group=1)` |
| `(?:...)` | a non-capturing group: grouping without a group number | `\\b(?:www\\.|https?://)` |

: How many and in what combination: quantifiers, alternatives and groups {#tbl-quantifiers}
:::
